paras: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of a Black man, known in Camden, South Carolina, as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivey's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was accused of killing F. M. McDowell, a white Camden man, with an axe on Thanksgiving morning, and he was shot while fleeing a citizens' party from Camden that was described as 'bent on lynching him' and that had posted the ferryman. He died the next morning after giving what the papers called a confession, and his death was reported by wire across the country.

According to the Charlotte papers, Ross had come to Camden about a year earlier, worked for McDowell, and was twice jailed over mortgaged property, which he gave as his motive. He was also wanted in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, for the killing of an older Black man, Bob Hennegan, about two years before, and the Governor had offered $200 for him.

On November 30 McDowell was found dead in a ditch near Ross's cabin about thirteen miles above Camden, and a Charleston dispatch said the county was being 'scoured' and that if caught 'it is not improbable that he will be lynched.' The Charlotte Observer put the turnout at three hundred citizens, who learned from Ross's brother Tom that 'Joe Wilson' was Joe Ross. Mounted men from Camden reached Charlotte saying they had traced him to within five miles of the city and were 'bent on lynching him if they can find him.'

Finding nothing near Charlotte, a party of twenty-five turned back into Lancaster County, picked up his trail near Six Mile Church, and drove him toward Ivy's mill, between Sugar Creek and the Catawba. There Ross asked Huntley to ferry him across; in the Charlotte Observer's account the ferryman, who knew him, invited him to the fire, then took up a musket and told him he was under arrest. When Ross pulled out the ramrod, Huntley shot him in the back above the thigh, tied him, and called in the pursuers, who were nearby.

The party carried him by wagon to the empty Hagan house and laid him on straw, where one of them wrote down his confession to the McDowell and Hennegan killings. He died about 3 a.m. by the Yorkville Enquirer and the Home and Democrat, or 5 a.m. by the Observer.

The body was taken by wagon to Lancaster and on to Camden, delivered, by the Observer's account, to the dead man's brother, and by the Home and Democrat's, to Ross's own brother. The Observer expected Huntley to collect the Governor's $200 reward, and no report of an inquest or of any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

Only white papers covered the case, first through a Charleston wire that ran in New York, Savannah and Alexandria under headlines such as 'The Perpetrator to be Lynched if Caught' and 'Murdered by a Negro.' A Charlotte wire of December 7 reported the killing under headings like 'A Negro Desperado Killed,' with the name variously printed 'Joe Row' and the ferryman 'Hunter.'

The Charlotte Observer's long story, reprinted in Raleigh as 'The Slayer Slain!', cast the pursuers as 'the avenging band' and said they had vowed to bring him back 'dead or alive, and they carried it back dead.' South Carolina weeklies ran the News and Courier's 'The Murder of a Murderer,' which noted plainly that the hunters 'had posted the ferryman,' and the Charlotte Home and Democrat ended its account with 'Thus ends the career of a desperate murderer.'

The Observer and Yorkville accounts say the struggle began when Huntley announced an arrest, while the Rock Hill dispatch says it began because the ferryman refused to take Ross across; both versions come from the pursuers' side. Early reports also named the fugitive Joe, Joseph, John or 'Jas.' Wilson before the later accounts identified him as Joe Ross.

reader.title: Killing of Joe Ross
bases: A citizens' pursuing party from Camden, said to be 'bent on lynching' the accused, hunted him across two states, and a ferryman it had 'posted' shot him during an attempted arrest; he died in the party's hands (A8, A13, A16, A17).

Ross was killed while fleeing a private pursuing party of 25 to 300 citizens that had declared it would bring him back 'dead or alive' and was 'bent on lynching him' (A8, A14), and the shooter was a ferryman the party had posted (A12, A16, A17). But the fatal shot was fired by one man who said he was arresting Ross and fired when Ross grabbed for the gun, a version that comes only from the pursuers' side (A13, A16); no officer or legal warrant is mentioned.

The Charlotte wire (A9-A11), the Charlotte Observer account (A13, A14), the Charlotte Home and Democrat (A19) and the Rock Hill News and Courier dispatch (A17) independently report the pursuit and the ferryman's killing of Ross, though they differ on how the encounter began.

framing.detail: The first wire forecast a lynching under the headline 'The Perpetrator to be Lynched if Caught' and called the killing 'brutal' without questioning the accusation.
The Charlotte Observer called the pursuers 'the avenging band', headed its story 'The Slayer Slain!', and said Huntley would likely draw the reward.
The Charlotte Home and Democrat closed with 'Thus ends the career of a desperate murderer.'
The News and Courier dispatch was headed 'The Murder of a Murderer' and noted that the hunters 'had posted the ferryman'.
